subtype: Stage 5: A bystander stops the chain [Response]
passage:
Monday. At the lunch table Bhavna leaned over. "Did you hear about Sunanda? Everyone's saying her family is moving because her father lost his job."
Binita put down her roti. "I don't want to talk about this. It's her business."
Bhavna rolled her eyes and moved seats.
Wednesday. Two girls tried again in the bus line. "Binita, you know Sunanda, right? Is it true?"
"I'm not passing it on," Binita said, though her ears felt hot.
The next Monday. Nobody was whispering any more. The story had run out of people to carry it. Sunanda sat at Binita's table and shared her mango slices, not knowing exactly why this was the one table that felt safe.

qa.q: What did Binita say when Bhavna asked about Sunanda on Monday?
qa.a: She said, "I don't want to talk about this. It's her business."

qa.q: How did Binita feel in the bus line when the girls asked again?
qa.a: She felt awkward and a bit embarrassed, with hot ears, but determined not to pass the story on.

qa.q: Why did Binita's refusal matter for the rumour?
qa.a: A rumour needs people to carry it; by refusing every time, Binita helped the story run out of carriers within a week.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunanda to sit at Binita's table?
qa.a: Sunanda feels safe there without quite knowing why, because nobody at that table is whispering about her family.

grounding: Shows a classmate refusing to repeat a rumour, which helps the story die out for lack of people to carry it.

passage: Worried about the whispering in your class, Uma? Let your old Elizabeth Aunty tell you about my Class 4, long ago. A story went round that little Sophia's father was in prison. It wasn't true, and she stopped eating her lunch. I didn't shout, and I didn't say her name. I asked the class, "Has anyone ever said something untrue about you? How did it feel?" Hands went up, one by one. Then I said, "Words can hurt like a push. If you hear a story about someone, bring it to me." At lunch I told Sophia quietly, "You can talk to me or to Mrs Rao any time." She came that same afternoon. The next week a boy stood up and said calmly, "That story is false." Nobody laughed at him.

qa.q: What story went round about Sophia?
qa.a: A story went round that Sophia's father was in prison.

qa.q: How was Sophia feeling when she stopped eating her lunch?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and ashamed by the false story, too upset to eat.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make with the class, and why did it help?
qa.a: She talked about how words hurt without naming Sophia, so nobody was shamed, and gave the children and Sophia a trusted adult to go to.

qa.q: What might the boy have felt when he stood up and said, 'That story is false'?
qa.a: He may have felt nervous but brave, and then steadier when nobody laughed at him for saying the truth calmly.

grounding: Shows a teacher addressing a rumour with the class without naming the girl, offering her a trusted adult, and a child learning that calm truth beats whispering.

passage:
Monday. Shankar saw Nisha and Farhan walk into first period ten minutes late, together, both a little breathless. Mrs Pillai marked them late without a word. Shankar's brain lit up. Together? Late? Something's going on.
Tuesday. He watched them all day. Farhan lent Nisha a pen. She laughed at something he said. Each tiny thing clicked into the picture Shankar had already drawn. He imagined telling the group and everyone turning to him: "How do you always know stuff, man?"
Thursday. At the bus stop Kishore asked, "Anything interesting this week?" Shankar opened his mouth, the story ready and polished. Then Kishore added, "Oh, did you hear Nisha and Farhan got stuck at the railway crossing on Monday? Same bus." Shankar shut his mouth. His big fact had only been a guess wearing a costume.

qa.q: Why were Nisha and Farhan late on Monday?
qa.a: They got stuck at the railway crossing on the same bus.

qa.q: What did Shankar want when he imagined telling the group?
qa.a: He wanted to feel important and connected, excited at the thought of everyone turning to him as the one who always knows.

qa.q: What could Shankar remember the next time a guess feels like news?
qa.a: He could separate what he actually saw, two people arriving late, from the story he added, and hold back until he knows the real reason.

qa.q: What would change for Nisha and Farhan if Shankar had told the group on Tuesday?
qa.a: They could have faced teasing and whispers about a relationship that did not exist, all because of a shared bus delay.

grounding: Shows a teen guessing at a relationship between two classmates who arrive late, with the wish to be first with news making the guess feel like fact.

passage: It was one line. That's what I keep telling myself. Last October I typed in our class group, "Amandeep and Rhea came out of the library together AGAIN, wedding when?" and added a laughing emoji. I thought it was funny for about four seconds. Within ten minutes someone had screenshotted it into another group. By evening someone else had added that they had been seen holding hands at the bus stop, which I never said and which, as far as I know, never happened. By morning there was a photo of them edited with hearts. I deleted my message at 11 p.m., panicking. It didn't matter. The screenshots were already everywhere, like seeds in the wind. Amandeep didn't come to class that Friday. On Monday our class teacher called me in and said, "Asif, tell me what happened." I told her everything. I still think about how fast my one line stopped being mine.

qa.q: What did Asif add to the line in the class group?
qa.a: Asif added a laughing emoji.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when deleting the message at 11 p.m.?
qa.a: Asif was panicking and guilty, realising the joke had grown into something false and hurtful that could not be taken back.

qa.q: What could Asif have done the moment the first screenshot appeared?
qa.a: Asif could have posted a clear correction, asked people not to forward it, and told a teacher straight away, rather than only deleting the line late at night.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have been going through that Friday?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably embarrassed and hurt by the edited photo and invented details, perhaps staying home to avoid the stares.

grounding: Shows a guess posted in a group chat with a laughing emoji being screenshotted and embellished faster than any correction could follow.

passage:
Dear Kiran Didi,
Something's been bothering me and I can't say it at home. Our class group has been going wild since Monday. Asif posted that Priyanka copied in the chemistry test, and now people keep adding "proof": a blurry photo, a "someone saw her".
Sixty-two people are in that group. I've read every message. So have most of us, I think; you can see the little seen-by list. Nobody has written, "This isn't fair." I typed it twice and deleted it twice. I kept thinking, if I say something, next week it'll be me.
But when nobody says anything, it looks as if all sixty-two of us believe it. Priyanka sits two seats from me. She hasn't looked up in class for two days.
What would you do?
Tanuja

qa.q: How many people are in the class group?
qa.a: Sixty-two people are in that group.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja type 'This isn't fair' and then delete it twice?
qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy about the rumour but scared of becoming the next target by speaking up.

qa.q: What small step could Tanuja take that doesn't mean confronting the whole group?
qa.a: Tanuja could message Priyanka privately to show support, refuse to forward anything, and tell a teacher as well as Kiran Didi what is happening.

qa.q: What is it like for Priyanka while the group stays silent?
qa.a: Priyanka seems isolated and ashamed, not looking up for two days, and the silence may make it seem to her that everyone believes the story.

grounding: Shows a classmate reading a rumour in a group chat, feeling uneasy but staying silent out of fear, and how that silence makes the rumour look believed.

passage: In Bhadrachalam, the rumour reached Shreya's house before she did: that she had been seen alone with Kishore from the next street behind the temple fair. She had only asked him the time. At school, boys hummed film songs when she passed, and girls she'd known since Class 1 moved their bags so she couldn't sit. At home Chachi said, "People are talking. A girl must think of the family's name," and Chacha suggested she stay home "for a few days, until it settles." Shreya didn't argue. For three days she lay facing the wall. On the third afternoon her maths teacher, Mr Varghese, came to the house. He sat with her parents on the verandah and said, "Shreya has done nothing wrong. Staying away is a warning sign, not a solution. Let's meet the headmistress tomorrow morning, together." Listening from the doorway, Shreya breathed out properly for the first time in days.

qa.q: What had Shreya actually done at the temple fair?
qa.a: She had only asked Kishore the time.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling during the three days she lay facing the wall?
qa.a: She felt isolated, ashamed and hopeless after the stares, the humming and the pressure at home, even though she had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: Why was Mr Varghese's visit the right step at this stage?
qa.a: He treated her staying away as a warning sign, told her family plainly she had done nothing wrong, and set up a meeting with the headmistress for the next morning.

qa.q: How might Chachi see the situation?
qa.a: Chachi seems worried about what people say and the family's name, and may not yet see how much the pressure is hurting Shreya.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl stared at and whispered about, pressured at home over reputation and staying away from school, and an adult treating that as a warning to act.

passage:
In Kalimpong, the school bus wound down the hill while Elizabeth stared at her phone, eyes wet. Someone in the Class 10 group had posted that she'd been sent home drunk from the Christmas programme. She had been sent home with a fever.
"I'm going to write a long message and tell everyone they're liars," Elizabeth said, thumbs shaking.
Dolma put a hand over the screen. "Wait. If you fight in the group, they'll screenshot that too."
Instead Dolma messaged the two boys who had shared it, separately: "That is not true. Please delete it." One did within minutes.
At the next stop, Dolma said, "Let's go to Lepcha Ma'am before assembly. I'll come with you." They went. Lepcha Ma'am listened, wrote down the names, and phoned Elizabeth's mother before first period.

qa.q: Why had Elizabeth actually been sent home from the Christmas programme?
qa.a: She had been sent home with a fever.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling as she planned a long message calling everyone liars?
qa.a: She felt angry and hurt, with wet eyes and shaking thumbs, desperate to defend herself in public.

qa.q: Why did Dolma's approach work better than a public reply?
qa.a: Dolma corrected it privately with the sharers and took Elizabeth to a teacher, which slowed the spread without giving the group a fresh fight to screenshot.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's mother feel when Lepcha Ma'am phones her?
qa.a: She would probably be upset about the rumour but relieved that the school is taking it seriously and that Elizabeth had support.

grounding: Shows a calm friend asking sharers to delete a false rumour and helping the target go to a teacher instead of replying publicly.

passage:
Thursday night
Today felt almost normal. The principal spoke to the whole of Class 9 in assembly: the girl who made the fake post about me has been suspended for three days under the school rules, and the four who forwarded it have to do sessions with the counsellor. She didn't say my name, and I was grateful for that. Ms D'Souza said, "Forwarding is a choice. Every forward is a push." For once nobody looked at me.
At lunch Swati saved my seat like she has every day for three weeks, and Harleen and Mehr came to sit too. Three weeks ago I thought I'd never want to walk down that corridor again.
Tonight Mummy called me her brave girl, and I let myself believe it. I still check the group sometimes. But less. Gurpreet, you're getting there.

qa.q: What happened to the girl who made the fake post?
qa.a: She has been suspended for three days under the school rules.

qa.q: What does 'Today felt almost normal' suggest about how Gurpreet is feeling?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels relieved and steadier, supported by friends and the school after three weeks of dreading the corridor.

qa.q: What did the school do that helped both the target and the group?
qa.a: It applied its rules to the source, sent those who forwarded to the counsellor, kept Gurpreet's name out of assembly, and taught that every forward is a choice.

qa.q: How might Swati see these three weeks?
qa.a: Swati has saved Gurpreet's seat every day, so she probably feels loyal and closer, and glad to see things turning.

grounding: Shows a school dealing with the source of a rumour under its rules while the target recovers with support and loyal friends grow closer.

subtype: Stage 1: The bully picks a target [Actor]
passage:
At home in Melbourne, Jin's older brothers took the TV remote, the last dumpling and the front seat, every single time. Jin never won.
At school on Monday he watched the new girl, Nadia, drop her pencil case. Two boys stepped on it by accident. She just picked everything up, face red, and said nothing. Jin noticed that. He noticed how she ate lunch in the corner of the library steps, and how she never looked up when someone bumped her.
Something small and hungry woke up in him. Here, maybe, was someone smaller than him.
He grinned at his friends. "Watch this," he said, and walked towards the library steps.

qa.q: What did Nadia do when her pencil case was stepped on?
qa.a: She just picked everything up, face red, and said nothing.

qa.q: What does Jin want when he says 'Watch this' to his friends?
qa.a: He wants to feel powerful and admired for once, since at home he always feels small and never wins.

qa.q: How could a teacher or parent step in at this stage?
qa.a: An adult who notices could keep an eye on Nadia and give Jin real ways to feel strong and respected, before any teasing begins.

qa.q: What would change if Nadia knew why Jin was choosing her?
qa.a: She might see that it was about Jin's need to feel bigger, not about anything she did, which could ease any shame she felt.

grounding: Shows a child who feels powerless at home picking a quiet classmate who doesn't fight back, out of his own need for power and admiration.

passage: In Class 4, I, Karthik, was the boy who gave Vishal his nickname: "Chashmish", because of his thick glasses. I said it once, softly, just to see. He went pink. A few kids laughed. So the next day I said it louder. Then I bumped his elbow in the lunch line, and when his dal spilled, the whole row laughed. Nobody told me to stop. The teacher was busy at her desk. By Friday I hid his school bag behind the water tank, and I felt like a king watching him search. Now I'm eleven and I understand: the laughing was what kept me going. Vishal never laughed once.

qa.q: Where did Karthik hide Vishal's school bag?
qa.a: He hid it behind the water tank.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel watching Vishal search for his bag?
qa.a: He felt powerful, like a king, because the laughing audience made the cruelty seem worth it.

qa.q: At what point could someone have stopped this, and how?
qa.a: On the very first day, when a few kids laughed at the nickname, a classmate or the teacher could have said stop and checked on Vishal before it grew.

qa.q: What was it like for Vishal during that week?
qa.a: Vishal was probably embarrassed and scared, going pink, losing his dal and searching for his bag, and he never laughed once.

grounding: Shows a child testing cruelty with a nickname, a nudge and a hidden bag, and learning from laughter and silence to go further.
